# Vamos Taxi — what we still need from you

This is everything we cannot finish without you. Work through it in one sitting if you can —
each item says plainly what it is for and what stays unfinished until you answer it. A blank
is a decision, not a delay: if you genuinely don't know yet, write "I don't know yet" in the
answer line rather than leaving it empty. That tells us something real; an empty line does not.

## What blocks launch

Six things stop the site from going live. Everything else in this document matters, but these
six are the reason we cannot flip the switch without them.

1. **The price matrix and its surcharges (question 11).** Nothing can go live while every fare
   on the site reads a placeholder amount — this is the one answer that turns checkout on.
2. **Your registered company details (questions 1–3).** The legal pages cannot lawfully publish
   without your real company name, address and registration number.
3. **The driver-no-show refund share and the remaining cancellation numbers (questions 19–23).**
   These are promises we make to a paying customer the moment they book — we cannot state a
   promise we have not confirmed with you.
4. **Your two free waiting allowances and what happens after them (questions 16–18).** The site
   currently states an allowance as settled fact in several places while the page that is
   supposed to own that fact still shows a gap — this has to close before launch, not after.
5. **Which analytics tool you want (question 35).** Nothing can be wired one way or the other
   until this lands, and it also decides what the cookie banner offers.
6. **Confirming the company details already sitting in our booking system (question 10).** Five
   values look like real company data today; we need you to say whether they are.

## How we handle your customers' data

The choice below is the launch blocker in this section; the rest are retention periods, which
matter for the privacy page but do not stop go-live on their own.

**35. Which analytics tool do you want us to use — Cloudflare Web Analytics, or PostHog?**

Cloudflare Web Analytics collects nothing personal and needs no cookie consent at all.
PostHog gives you a much richer picture of how people move through the booking flow, but it
needs a cookie and a consent prompt to do it. Nothing is wired to either one until you choose,
and the choice changes what the cookie banner offers.

- **Our recommendation:** only you can answer this — it is a genuine trade-off between richer
  product data and a simpler consent experience, and that trade is yours to make, not ours.
- **What your old site said:** the old site ran Google Analytics, which does not fit our stack
  either way and is not one of the two live options.
- **If you leave this blank:** nothing is wired, the cookie banner cannot list a real analytics
  entry, and the privacy page keeps a labelled gap in four places.
- **Needs translating once given:** no — this is an internal tooling choice, not printed copy.
- **Your answer:**

**37. How long should we keep finance records — invoices and payment records?**

- **Our recommendation:** ten years, set by the Swiss Code of Obligations, Article 958f, which
  requires a business to keep its accounting books and vouchers for ten years from the end of
  the financial year they belong to. This is the one retention figure in this section a named
  law genuinely fixes.
- **What your old site said:** the old site never published this.
- **If you leave this blank:** the privacy page keeps a labelled gap where this belongs, and we
  fall back to the legal minimum above rather than guess a shorter figure.
- **Needs translating once given:** no — a retention period is a number, not translated text.
- **Your answer:**

**38. How long should we keep server logs?**

- **Our recommendation:** only you can answer this — no law we can point to fixes an exact
  number of days for a server log; both Swiss and EU data-protection law only say to keep data
  no longer than needed, which is a principle, not a figure.
- **What your old site said:** the old site never published this.
- **If you leave this blank:** the privacy page keeps a labelled gap where this belongs.

**40. How quickly do we commit to responding to a customer who asks what data we hold on them?**

- **Our recommendation:** one month, set by Article 12(3) of the GDPR, which gives a business
  one calendar month to respond to a data-subject request, extendable by two further months for
  a genuinely complex one. Swiss data-protection law does not fix its own exact number of days,
  so lining up with the same one-month figure keeps one rule instead of two.
- **What your old site said:** the old site never published this.
- **If you leave this blank:** the privacy page keeps a labelled gap where this belongs, and we
  fall back to the one-month figure above rather than guess a shorter one.
- **Needs translating once given:** yes — short phrase, four languages.

## What we are handling ourselves

So you can see what is already off your plate, and object if we have got something wrong.

- The real names of the cookies our systems set, and how long each one lasts — these arrive
  automatically with the systems that create them, and are facts about our build rather than
  something you choose.
- How long a signed-in session lasts, how long a sign-in or password-reset link stays valid,
  and the rules for a verification code.
- The format of your booking reference number.
- How currency amounts are displayed on screen.
- Where your customer database physically sits — already pinned to the data centre closest to
  Zürich, for both speed and data-protection reasons.
- A set of build decisions made during this stage of the project: the booking reference format,
  how currency is priced versus displayed, how a round-trip booking is structured, where the
  booking system's data is processed, and which planned features are being held back for a
  later release. None of these change anything a customer or a member of your staff sees or
  types.

## What needs translating once you answer

Every question above already tells you, item by item, whether its answer needs translating. In
short: short values — a fee, a duration, a name, a short phrase — become whole phrases in
German, French and Arabic, not a bare number with a unit stuck on afterwards, and we handle that
translation as part of our own build work once you give us the value.

The long-form legal text is different. Once your company details, prices and policies are
confirmed, the actual clauses on the terms, privacy, cancellation, cookies and imprint pages
need to be written up in full and then translated by a professional legal translator, not
machine-translated — these pages carry legal effect, and a translation error there is a real
liability, not a typo. Until that professional translation is complete, the affected legal pages
will say plainly which languages they currently exist in, rather than pretend to offer all four.
